analysis.one_liner: Gives hourly workers the right to request stable schedules and requires two weeks' advance notice of shifts.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 21 senators, never received a committee hearing or a vote in the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let any employee at a company with 15 or more workers ask for changes to their schedule — for a health condition, caregiving, school, or a second job — and require the employer to discuss the request and give written reasons for any denial. For hourly workers in retail, food service, cleaning, hotels, and warehouses, it would require work schedules to be posted 14 days ahead, with extra pay for last-minute changes, cancelled shifts, split shifts, and back-to-back 'clopening' shifts. Workers could decline on-call shifts and shifts starting less than 11 hours after their last one ended. It also bans employers from retaliating against workers who make requests, and lets the Labor Department or workers themselves sue to enforce it.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly, non-exempt workers in retail, food service, cleaning, hospitality, and warehouse jobs — occupations where the bill's findings cite surveys showing about two-thirds of workers get less than two weeks' schedule notice and one in three has worked a 'clopening' shift. Workers juggling child care, medical appointments, school, or a second job gain the right to request predictable hours without fear of being fired or having their hours cut. Workers of color, who the bill's findings say are more likely to face cancelled and on-call shifts, would be among the most affected.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly retail, food service, and warehouse workers

how_it_helps.text: Employees may request changes to hours, shift times, work location, advance notice, and hour-to-hour predictability, and the employer must engage in a good-faith interactive process and give written reasons for denials [S2].
For requests tied to a serious health condition, caregiving, education or training, or a second job, the employer must grant the request unless it has a 'bona fide business reason' [S2].

Covered-sector employers must post work schedules at least 14 days in advance, pay $75 per day for late schedules, and pay extra (predictability pay) for changes made with less than 14 days' notice or half-pay for cancelled scheduled hours [S2].
Employees may decline on-call shifts and shifts starting less than 11 hours after their previous shift, and must be paid extra for split shifts and for working less than 11 hours apart [S2].

Retaliation against workers who exercise these rights is unlawful, and workers can sue for lost wages, liquidated damages, and attorney's fees, with Labor Department enforcement and civil penalties for willful, repeated violations [S2].
The bill's findings cite survey data that about two-thirds of hourly retail and food service workers receive schedules with less than two weeks' notice and 65 percent want more stable schedules [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large retail, restaurant, hotel, warehouse, and cleaning employers, who would bear the cost of advance scheduling, predictability pay, split-shift and rest-period premiums, and $75-per-day penalties for late schedules. These costs could be passed to consumers through prices or absorbed through leaner staffing, and small chains near the 15-employee threshold would face new compliance and recordkeeping burdens.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large retail, restaurant, hotel, and warehouse employers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are real: predictability pay, split-shift premiums, $75-per-day penalties, and recordkeeping requirements fall on employers in low-margin industries like food service and retail, and some of that cost may reach consumers through higher prices [S2].

The 'bona fide business reason' denial standard is broad — it includes productivity loss, retraining costs, inability to meet customer demand, and insufficiency of work — so an employer can still refuse most requests with a documented reason [S2].

Unionized workplaces can be exempted if the collective bargaining agreement governs scheduling and expressly waives the Act's protections, which critics of such carve-outs argue leaves some of the most organized workers with weaker individual rights [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the benefits — two weeks' notice of shifts, pay for cancelled or last-minute changes, and the right to ask without retaliation — address a documented problem that destabilizes child care, second jobs, and public-benefit eligibility. The costs fall on employers and partly on consumers, and the bill's own findings cite a Gap Inc. pilot where more stable schedules were associated with higher sales and lower turnover, suggesting some costs are offset. The main honest criticism is that the request-granting requirement is soft: employers keep a wide 'bona fide business reason' escape hatch, so the strongest provisions are the notice and pay rules for the five named sectors rather than a general guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never held a hearing or markup, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Warren introduced the bill on September 19, 2023, joined by 20 cosponsors (19 Democrats and 1 Independent) [S1, S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S4].
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in retail, food service, hotels, warehouses, and cleaning, who avoid the scheduling, predictability-pay, and penalty requirements the bill would have imposed. Workers in unstable 'just-in-time' scheduling jobs gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent from Vermont; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: The bill would require 14-day advance schedules, predictability pay, and $75-per-day penalties for late schedules in retail sales occupations. Retail has been a center of just-in-time scheduling, and the bill was written to end that practice [S2].

Food preparation and serving workers are squarely covered: two-thirds report less than two weeks' notice and one in three has worked 'clopening' shifts. The bill would require advance notice, premiums for cancelled and split shifts, and rest between shifts [S2].
Warehouse employees would be covered-sector workers subject to the 14-day notice, predictability pay, and rest-period requirements [S2].
Hotel, motel, and inn employees are covered by definition and would face the same scheduling, pay-premium, and rest requirements [S2].
Janitors, maids, and cleaners are among the named covered occupations and would gain notice and predictability-pay rights their employers would have to fund [S2].
